rows.title: Lundy cabbage weevil
rows.evidence: Two invertebrate taxa are endemic to Lundy, with both feeding on the endemic Lundy cabbage (Coincya wrightii). These are the Lundy cabbage flea beetle (Psylliodes luridipennis), a species of leaf beetle (family Chrysomelidae) and the Lundy cabbage weevil (Ceutorhynchus insularis, formerly Ceutorhynchus contractus var. pallipes), a variety of true weevil (family Curculionidae).
rows.summary: The Lundy cabbage weevil (Ceutorhynchus insularis) is one of two invertebrate taxa endemic to Lundy, where it feeds on the Lundy cabbage. The Lundy cabbage flea beetle is already listed separately.

rows.title: Wood calamint
rows.evidence: In Britain, it is limited to a single site in the Isle of Wight, where it grows in ancient deciduous woodland on a chalk soil.
rows.summary: Wood calamint (Clinopodium menthifolium) is limited in Britain to a single site in the Isle of Wight. The photograph shows the species.

rows.title: Island knotweed
rows.evidence: In Britain it is restricted to scattered locations on the Isle of Skye and the Isle of Mull.
rows.summary: Island knotweed (Koenigia islandica) is restricted in Britain to the Isle of Skye and the Isle of Mull. The photograph shows the species.

rows.title: Island knotweed
rows.evidence: In Britain it is restricted to scattered locations on the Isle of Skye and the Isle of Mull.
rows.summary: Island knotweed (Koenigia islandica) is restricted in Britain to the Isle of Skye and the Isle of Mull. The photograph shows the species.

rows.title: Saxifraga rosacea subsp. hartii
rows.evidence: Saxifraga rosacea subsp. hartii: Arranmore Island.
rows.summary: The article gives Saxifraga rosacea subsp. hartii the range Arranmore Island, and gives the other subspecies ranges in continental Europe, Ireland, Iceland and the Faroes. The photograph shows Saxifraga rosacea.

rows.title: Scilly bee
rows.source_title: List of endemic species of the British Isles
rows.evidence: Bombus muscorum scyllonius (Richards), Scilly bee – a bumble bee, which in the 1960s was found on all the inhabited islands of the Isles of Scilly with the exception of Bryher, and currently is only known from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur.
rows.summary: The Scilly bee (Bombus muscorum scyllonius) is currently only known from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur. Great Arthur is not in the atlas.

rows.title: Scilly bee
rows.source_title: List of endemic species of the British Isles
rows.evidence: Bombus muscorum scyllonius (Richards), Scilly bee – a bumble bee, which in the 1960s was found on all the inhabited islands of the Isles of Scilly with the exception of Bryher, and currently is only known from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur.
rows.summary: The Scilly bee (Bombus muscorum scyllonius) is currently only known from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur. Great Arthur is not in the atlas.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence says the subspecies is found only in Ireland and the Isle of Man. It is not endemic to the Isle of Man, not named for it, and the sentence does not call the island a principal stronghold.
rows.title: Irish stoat
rows.source_title: List of endemic species of the British Isles
rows.evidence: Irish stoat — A subspecies of stoat found only in Ireland and the Isle of Man.
rows.summary: The Irish stoat is a subspecies of stoat found only in Ireland and the Isle of Man. The photograph shows a stoat (Mustela erminea).

rows.title: Portland sea lavender
rows.evidence: Portland sea lavender can be found on the higher sea cliffs; unique to Portland, it is one of the United Kingdom's rarest plants.
rows.summary: Portland sea lavender is unique to Portland. The photograph is identified as Limonium recurvum subsp. recurvum at Portland.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence names Great Arthur, and the atlas has Little Arthur only.
rows.title: Scilly bee
rows.source_title: List of endemic species of the British Isles
rows.evidence: Bombus muscorum scyllonius (Richards), Scilly bee – a bumble bee, which in the 1960s was found on all the inhabited islands of the Isles of Scilly with the exception of Bryher, and currently is only known from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur.

rows.reject_reason: The endemic list is a checklist line calling it a house mouse subspecies found only on Canna. The Canna article says the mice are believed to be a wood mouse subspecies. There is no species article.
rows.title: Canna mouse
rows.evidence: Because the mice on the island are believed to be a rare and distinct subspecies of woodmouse, a breeding population of mice was removed beforehand by the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS) so that the cull could use rodenticide.

rows.reject_reason: Within Scilly it only occurs on St Mary's, but the same article places the species on mainland Cornwall as well, so St Mary's is not the stronghold.
rows.title: Western ramping-fumitory
rows.evidence: Fumaria occidentalis is restricted to "the warmest districts in Cornwall", comprising the westernmost parts of mainland Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, from near Padstow around Land's End towards The Lizard. Within the Isles of Scilly, it only occurs on St. Mary's, although there are historical records of its occurrence on St. Martin's.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence names Teesdale and western Ireland. Neither is one atlas island.
rows.title: Spring gentian
rows.evidence: In northern Europe, it is very rare, confined to Teesdale in northern England and a handful of locations in western Ireland.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence names the Scottish mainland and the Orkney Islands. No one Orkney island is the stronghold.
rows.title: Erythranthe peregrina
rows.evidence: Making this species even more unusual, two separate populations of E. peregrina arose independently; one on the Scottish mainland and the Orkney Islands off the coast of northern Scotland, via genome duplication from local populations of E. × robertsii, a hybrid of Erythranthe guttata from western North America and Erythranthe lutea from the Andes of South America.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to the north of Ireland. Ireland is not an atlas island.
rows.title: Irish round-leaved hawkweed
rows.evidence: Hieracium hibernicyclicum, the Irish round-leaved hawkweed, is a species of hawkweed in the genus Hieracium, endemic to the north of Ireland.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to Ross Island near Killarney, which is not in the atlas. The following sentence gives a count of plants, so it is not stored.
rows.title: Scannell's whitebeam
rows.evidence: Hedlundia scannelliana, commonly known as Scannell's whitebeam, is a species of shrub or tree endemic to Ross Island near Killarney in southwest Ireland.

rows.reject_reason: Discovered on the island is not endemic, named for the island as a stronghold, or a principal stronghold. Epipactis sancta redirects to Epipactis dunensis, which the same paragraph says the plants were formerly identified as.
rows.title: Lindisfarne helleborine
rows.evidence: An orchid, the Lindisfarne helleborine, has been discovered on the island.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to the Shetland Islands. No one Shetland island is named.
rows.title: Shetland hawkweed
rows.evidence: The Shetland Hawkweed (Hieracium zetlandicum), endemic to the Shetland Islands.

rows.reject_reason: The subspecies is found in the Outer Hebrides and the Isle of Skye, and in western Ireland. Skye is not the stronghold.
rows.title: Hebridean song thrush
rows.evidence: T. p. hebridensis, described by British ornithologist William Eagle Clarke in 1913, is a mainly sedentary (non-migratory) form found in the Outer Hebrides and Isle of Skye in Scotland, and western Ireland.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence calls Clethrionomys glareolus caesarius an endemic subspecies, and it does not name Jersey. No other Wikipedia page states the range.
rows.title: Jersey bank vole
rows.evidence: Four species of small mammal are considered native: the wood mouse, bank vole (an endemic subspecies Clethrionomys glareolus caesarius), lesser white-toothed shrew and crowned shrew.

rows.reject_reason: Found only in the Beinn Eighe nature reserve, which is not an island.
rows.title: Northern prongwort
rows.evidence: It is endemic to Scotland, where it is found only in the Beinn Eighe nature reserve.

rows.reject_reason: Known from Shetland and Norway. Shetland is the archipelago, and the species has no article of its own.
rows.title: Viking prongwort
rows.evidence: A closely related species, described in 2012 as Herbertus norenus and known as "Viking prongwort", is known from Shetland and Norway and was formerly confused with H. borealis.

rows.reject_reason: The single-location list is an incomplete table from 2008, not a sentence, and the species has no article. The table says Isle of Lewis. The atlas island is Lewis and Harris.
rows.title: Euphrasia campbelliae
rows.source_title: List of species occurring in Britain at a single location
rows.evidence: The eyebright Euphrasia campbelliae is listed at the Isle of Lewis, with formerly found elsewhere marked No.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to Devon and Cornwall, not to one island.
rows.title: Vigur's eyebright
rows.evidence: Euphrasia vigursii, also known by its common names of Vigur's eyebright or Cornish eyebright, is an endangered annual of the eyebright family which is endemic to Devon and Cornwall.

rows.reject_reason: The British subspecies is given as southern Great Britain, not one island.
rows.title: Slender centaury
rows.evidence: Centaurium tenuiflorum subsp. anglicum T.C.G.Rich & McVeigh – southern Great Britain.

rows.reject_reason: The range is a strip of shore on the Menai Strait at Nantporth Nature Reserve. That shore is not an atlas island.
rows.title: Aria arvonicola
rows.evidence: It is native to a restricted area along the shore of the Menai Strait in North Wales.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to the Great Orme, which is a headland, not an atlas island.
rows.title: Wild cotoneaster
rows.evidence: Cotoneaster cambricus (wild cotoneaster; Welsh: Creigafal y Gogarth "rock apple of Gogarth") is a species of Cotoneaster endemic to the Great Orme peninsula in north Wales.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to Scotland, not to one island.
rows.title: Newman's lady-fern
rows.evidence: Athyrium flexile, commonly known as Newman's lady-fern or the flexile lady fern, is a taxon of fern which is endemic to Scotland.

rows.reject_reason: Subspecies norvegica includes west and northwest Scotland, the Shetland Isles, western Ireland, Scandinavia and Iceland. Subspecies anglica is the Yorkshire Dales. No one island is named.
rows.title: Norwegian sandwort
rows.evidence: Arenaria norvegica subsp. norvegica is found in west and northwest Scotland, the Shetland Isles, western Ireland, and Scandinavia and Iceland.

rows.reject_reason: An occurrence list of nine Orkney islands. Mainland is already accepted. The article says the per-island subspecies names are a past treatment, not a current endemic on each island.
rows.title: Orkney vole
rows.evidence: The Orkney vole occurs on nine islands of the group, Mainland: Sanday, Westray, Rousay, South Ronaldsay, Burray, Eday, Shapinsay, and Stronsay.

rows.reject_reason: The centre of distribution is Dorset, Wiltshire, and the Isle of Wight. The island is not the stronghold.
rows.title: Early gentian
rows.evidence: Gentianella anglica is endemic to Great Britain and its centre of distribution is in Dorset, Wiltshire, and the Isle of Wight.

rows.reject_reason: One of three locations on the Isle of Wight is not a principal stronghold.
rows.title: Duke of Burgundy
rows.evidence: The Duke of Burgundy fritillary occurs on the grassland, in one of only three locations on the Isle of Wight where it occurs.

rows.reject_reason: Flat Holm is given as an example of the soils the aggregate grows on, not as a stronghold of one endemic sea-lavender.
rows.title: Rock sea-lavender
rows.evidence: Growing 10–70 cm tall from a rhizome, Limonium binervosum flourishes in saline soils, so are therefore common near the western coasts and in salt marshes, and also on saline, gypsum and alkaline soils such as found on Flat Holm island in Wales, UK.

rows.reject_reason: Endemic to Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands together, and in Britain it follows a line from Devon to Orkney. The Isle of Man is not the stronghold.
rows.title: Purple ramping-fumitory
rows.evidence: Fumaria purpurea has only been recorded in Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man and the Channel Isles (an area sometimes referred to by naturalists as the British Isles), which makes it endemic to this area.

rows.reject_reason: Recorded on the mainland and on Skye and Orkney. Skye is not the stronghold, and Orkney is not one island.
rows.title: Mountain bearberry
rows.evidence: Mountain bearberry, recorded at only a few mainland locations, and on Skye and Orkney.

rows.reject_reason: The rats were on the Shiant Isles as a group, and the islands were later declared free of the black rat. The wording that calls them the stronghold also gives counts, so that sentence is not stored.
rows.island_name: Shiant Islands (Garbh Eilean, Eilean an Tighe, Eilean Mhuire + Galta Mòr/Beag)
rows.title: Black rat
rows.source_title: Flora and fauna of the Outer Hebrides
rows.evidence: The Shiant Isles were home to a colony of black rats, which may originally have come ashore from a shipwreck. The Shiants were officially declared free of the black rat.

rows.reject_reason: Naturalised at one site on Skye. It is not native there.
rows.title: Peltaria alliacea
rows.evidence: It has become naturalized at a single location on the Isle of Skye in the U.K.

rows.reject_reason: The sentence hedges a Skye fish as the same or a very similar species. Orkney charr is already accepted on Hoy.
rows.title: Orkney charr
rows.evidence: The same or a very similar fish has been observed in Loch Mealt, on the Isle of Skye.
